questions.stem: A 67 year old man has had three episodes of central chest tightness at rest over the past 24 hours, each lasting 20 minutes. GTN spray did not relieve the latest episode. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg. His ECG (see item resources) is shown. High-sensitivity troponin is 8 ng/L at 0 hours and 9 ng/L at 3 hours (reference <14 ng/L).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG on arrival
visual.caption: Horizontal ST depression in I and V4 to V6, no ST elevation.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rest pain, ST depression and a normal, flat troponin mean ischaemia without necrosis: unstable angina.

clues: 8 ng/L at 0 hours and 9 ng/L at 3 hours
steps.x: Ischaemic pain **at rest**, not relieved by GTN, with ST depression but **normal serial troponin**.

elim: Pericarditis gives sharp positional pain and saddle ST elevation, not ST depression.
NSTEMI needs a raised troponin; both values are normal.
There is no ST elevation and troponin is normal.
Stable angina is exertional and relieved by rest or GTN; this is at rest and GTN failed.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** Rest pain + ischaemic ECG + normal troponin = unstable angina.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman had a myocardial infarction 4 years ago. For 2 weeks her exertional chest pain has come on with less and less activity, and this morning it occurred while she was watching television. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. Her ECG shows T-wave inversion in V4 to V6. Serial high-sensitivity troponin is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A crescendo pattern ending in rest pain in someone with previous IHD, with normal troponin, is unstable angina.

steps.x: **Crescendo** angina progressing to **rest** pain, previous IHD, ischaemic T waves, troponin normal.

elim: No murmur or syncope is described, and this would not explain a sudden crescendo to rest pain.
Troponin is normal, so there is no necrosis.
Vasospastic angina gives transient ST elevation in young patients, often smokers, not a crescendo pattern.
Pain coming on with less exertion and then at rest is no longer stable.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** Crescendo or rest angina with normal troponin = unstable angina.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with central chest pain at rest is assessed in the Emergency Department. His ECG shows ST depression in V3 to V6. A diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome is made. Serial high-sensitivity troponin is awaited.
questions.q: Which result would most strongly support unstable angina rather than NSTEMI?
o: Rise in troponin above the 99th centile
Troponin within the normal range on serial testing
questions.e: Troponin stays normal in unstable angina; any rise above the 99th centile means NSTEMI.

clues: ST depression in V3 to V6
steps.x: An ACS with no ST elevation: UA versus NSTEMI hinges on **troponin**.

elim: D-dimer helps exclude PE; it does not separate UA from NSTEMI.
Echo can be normal in both.
A rise means necrosis: that is NSTEMI.
ECG changes can resolve in both; troponin is the discriminator.

steps.x: **E. Troponin within the normal range on serial testing.** UA and NSTEMI are separated by troponin alone.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has had 40 minutes of central chest heaviness at rest radiating to his jaw. He is sweaty. His ECG shows T-wave inversion in II, III and aVF, and his troponin is normal at 0 and 3 hours. He is diagnosed with unstable angina.
questions.q: Which feature of his history is the most important risk factor for this diagnosis?
questions.e: Previous ischaemic heart disease (here a previous stent) is the main risk factor for unstable angina.

clues: troponin is normal at 0 and 3 hours
steps.x: Confirmed UA; pick the option that shows **existing coronary disease**.

elim: Not a recognised coronary risk factor in a relative.
A differential for chest pain, not a risk factor.
Irrelevant to coronary disease.
A risk factor for PE, not ACS.

steps.x: **A. Coronary stent inserted 6 years ago.** Previous IHD is the main risk factor for UA.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has had 30 minutes of central chest pain at rest. Her ECG shows ST depression in V4 to V6. Serial troponin is normal. She is diagnosed with unstable angina.
questions.q: Which additional feature is most likely to be present?
o: Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
Tearing pain radiating to the back
questions.e: Autonomic features (sweating, nausea) commonly accompany ischaemic rest pain in UA.

clues: ST depression in V4 to V6
steps.x: Ischaemic chest pain: expect **autonomic** features, SOB, radiation to arm or jaw.

elim: Suggests infection, not ischaemia.
A feature of pericarditis.
Suggests musculoskeletal pain.
Suggests aortic dissection.

steps.x: **D. Sweating and nausea.** Sweating and nausea accompany ischaemic pain.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has had chest pain at rest for 25 minutes that eased with morphine. His ECG shows ST depression in V5 and V6. High-sensitivity troponin is 5 ng/L at 0 hours and 6 ng/L at 3 hours (reference <14 ng/L). His registrar explains this is an acute coronary syndrome without myocardial necrosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: ACS without necrosis, troponin normal, is unstable angina.

clues: chest pain at rest for 25 minutes
5 ng/L at 0 hours and 6 ng/L at 3 hours
steps.x: An **ACS** with **normal troponin**: no necrosis.

elim: Vasospasm classically gives transient ST elevation; this is rest ACS with ST depression.
NSTEMI involves necrosis with raised troponin.
Stable angina is not an ACS and is not rest pain.
Takotsubo usually raises troponin and follows emotional stress, often in women.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** ACS + no necrosis = unstable angina.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man was admitted 12 hours ago with unstable angina; his troponin at 0 and 3 hours was normal. He now has severe crushing chest pain. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. A repeat ECG shows new ST elevation in V1 to V4.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Unstable angina can progress to full MI if the partial thrombus propagates to complete occlusion; new anterior ST elevation is a STEMI.

clues: admitted 12 hours ago with unstable angina
new ST elevation in V1 to V4
steps.x: Known UA, new **territorial ST elevation**: the thrombus has **occluded** the artery.

elim: Pericarditis gives widespread saddle ST elevation, not territorial V1 to V4.
No tearing back pain or BP difference.
Would not produce new ST elevation.
PE does not cause territorial anterior ST elevation.

steps.x: **D. Progression to myocardial infarction.** UA can progress to MI: that is why it is high-risk.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman admitted with unstable angina 2 days ago becomes breathless and confused. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 78/50 mmHg, and her peripheries are cold and clammy. There are bilateral basal crackles. Her urine output has been 10 mL/hour for 3 hours.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hypotension, cold peripheries, pulmonary oedema and oliguria after an ACS mean cardiogenic shock, a complication of unstable angina.

clues: admitted with unstable angina 2 days ago
steps.x: Hypotension + **cold** peripheries + **pulmonary congestion** + low urine output.

elim: No drug exposure, rash or wheeze, and the peripheries are cold, not warm.
Basal crackles point to pump failure, not volume loss.
No fever or source, and sepsis usually gives warm peripheries early.
Transient with bradycardia; this is persistent hypotension with organ hypoperfusion.

steps.x: **B. Cardiogenic shock.** Cold, wet and hypotensive after ACS = cardiogenic shock.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man admitted with unstable angina yesterday says he feels his heart racing. His pulse rate is 146 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 124/78 mmHg. His chest pain has not returned. Serial troponin remains normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG?
questions.e: Arrhythmias are a complication of UA; a fast irregularly irregular pulse is AF.

steps.x: Palpitations with an **irregularly irregular** pulse after ACS: an arrhythmia complication.

elim: Gives a slow regular pulse, not 146 bpm irregularly irregular.
Gives a slow, regularly irregular pattern.
Sinus rhythm is regular.
VF is pulseless; he has a BP.

steps.x: **A. Atrial fibrillation.** Irregularly irregular = AF.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has had central chest pain at rest for 35 minutes, radiating to her left arm, with palpitations. She has had a previous coronary stent. Her ECG (see item resources) is shown. Troponin at 0 and 3 hours is normal.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: T-wave inversion V1 to V4, no ST elevation.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: T-wave inversion with rest pain and normal troponin in a patient with known IHD is unstable angina.

clues: chest pain at rest for 35 minutes
Troponin at 0 and 3 hours is normal
steps.x: Rest pain, **ischaemic T-wave inversion**, known IHD, troponin normal.

elim: Brugada shows coved ST elevation in V1 to V2, not anterior T-wave inversion with rest pain.
Normal troponin excludes it.
No pleuritic pain, hypoxia or risk factors; previous stent points to coronary disease.
Stable angina does not occur at rest.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** The ECG in UA may show ST depression, T inversion or be normal.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has had 20 minutes of central chest pain at rest that has now settled. His ECG (see item resources) was taken within 10 minutes of arrival. His high-sensitivity troponin is 7 ng/L at 0 hours and 7 ng/L at 3 hours (reference <14 ng/L). He has had two angioplasties in the past.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A normal ECG does not exclude unstable angina; the diagnosis is clinical with normal troponin.

clues: 7 ng/L at 0 hours and 7 ng/L at 3 hours
steps.x: Typical rest pain in known IHD; ECG normal; troponin normal.

elim: There is no chest wall tenderness, and he has a strong coronary history with rest pain.
Troponin is normal.
No positional pain or ST elevation.
The ECG is normal.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** A normal ECG does not rule out UA.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man arrives in the Emergency Department by ambulance with 30 minutes of central chest pain at rest. He has had a previous MI. His pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 150/92 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Every patient with suspected ACS needs a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes to identify STEMI and ischaemic changes.

steps.x: Suspected **ACS**: the first test is the one that finds a STEMI.

elim: May help exclude other causes but does not identify STEMI.
Not an emergency first test in suspected ACS.
Not the first test; the ECG decides immediate management.
Contraindicated in active rest pain.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes.** ECG within 10 minutes in suspected ACS.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has had chest pain at rest for 40 minutes. Her ECG shows ST depression in V4 to V6. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. She is given aspirin 300 mg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to distinguish unstable angina from NSTEMI?
questions.e: Diagnosis is clinical assessment plus ECG and troponin; a normal serial troponin means UA, a rise means NSTEMI.

clues: chest pain at rest for 40 minutes
ST depression in V4 to V6
steps.x: Ischaemic rest pain with ST depression: is there **necrosis**?

elim: Shows anatomy, not whether necrosis has occurred.
Less sensitive and specific than troponin.
Used for PE, not ACS.
Wall motion can be abnormal in both.

steps.x: **E. Serial high-sensitivity troponin.** Serial troponin separates UA from NSTEMI.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with unstable angina has settled on aspirin, ticagrelor and fondaparinux. Troponin at 0 and 3 hours is normal. The team must decide between early coronary angiography and conservative management.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate tool to guide this decision?
questions.e: The GRACE score stratifies ischaemic risk in UA/NSTEMI and guides early invasive versus conservative management.

clues: early coronary angiography and conservative management
steps.x: A **risk stratification** decision in NSTE-ACS.

elim: Estimates stroke risk in AF.
Assesses pneumonia severity.
Estimates bleeding risk on anticoagulation, not ischaemic risk.
Estimates the probability of PE or DVT.

steps.x: **C. GRACE score.** GRACE guides invasive versus conservative.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman was admitted with chest pain at rest. Her ECG was normal and troponin was normal at 0 and 3 hours. Her GRACE score is low and she is managed conservatively. Before discharge her team want a non-invasive test to look for coronary artery disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: CT coronary angiography is the first-line diagnostic investigation for angina; invasive angiography is for high-risk patients.

clues: non-invasive test to look for coronary artery disease
steps.x: Low risk, managed conservatively, needs a **non-invasive anatomical** test.

elim: Not the first-line anatomical test for angina.
Does not show the coronary arteries.
No longer first-line for diagnosing angina.
Reserved for high-risk patients; she is low risk.

steps.x: **C. CT coronary angiography.** CTCA is first-line for angina.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man with central chest pain at rest has ST depression in V4 to V6. His high-sensitivity troponin trend is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: High-sensitivity troponin
visual.caption: Normal and flat: no myocardial necrosis.

questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation?
questions.e: A flat, normal troponin shows the reduction in flow was too brief or too small to cause necrosis: unstable angina.

clues: ST depression in V4 to V6
steps.x: Ischaemic ECG but **troponin normal and flat**.

elim: That would give ST elevation and a large troponin rise.
That describes NSTEMI, with a troponin rise.
Rest pain with ST depression is ischaemic.
There is no rise.

steps.x: **A. Ischaemia without myocardial necrosis.** Normal troponin = ischaemia without necrosis.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has unstable angina. His ECG shows ST depression in V5 and V6 and troponin is normal at 0 and 3 hours. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 142/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He has no bleeding risk and normal renal function.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Initial UA treatment is aspirin 300 mg plus a P2Y12 inhibitor and fondaparinux; thrombolysis has no role.

steps.x: Confirmed NSTE-ACS: **DAPT plus anticoagulation**; no hypoxia.

elim: Thrombolysis is for STEMI when PCI is unavailable, never NSTE-ACS.
Oxygen is not needed at 97% and he needs DAPT and anticoagulation.
Needs a 300 mg loading dose, a second antiplatelet and anticoagulation.
Not used in ACS.

steps.x: **C. Aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor and fondaparinux.** Aspirin 300 mg + clopidogrel/ticagrelor + fondaparinux.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with unstable angina is receiving aspirin, clopidogrel and fondaparinux. She has ongoing central chest pain. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Symptom control in UA is GTN (and morphine if needed); oxygen only if hypoxic.

steps.x: Pain continues on DAPT and anticoagulation; saturation normal.

elim: Oxygen is only given if SpO2 is below 94%.
No signs of fluid overload.
Not used for immediate pain relief at this dose.
Contraindicated in NSTE-ACS.

steps.x: **D. Sublingual GTN.** GTN for pain; oxygen only if SpO2 <94%.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with unstable angina has been given aspirin 300 mg and ticagrelor. His eGFR is 70 mL/min/1.73m² and he has no bleeding risk factors.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant to start?
questions.e: Fondaparinux is first-line anticoagulation in UA, with LMWH if it is unsuitable.

steps.x: DAPT given: now add **anticoagulation**.

elim: A DOAC, not the ACS anticoagulant of choice here.
Not used in acute coronary syndrome.
Kept for severe renal impairment or immediate angiography.
Not used in ACS.

steps.x: **C. Fondaparinux.** Fondaparinux first-line, LMWH if unsuitable.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with diabetes and chronic kidney disease has unstable angina. Her troponin is normal but she has recurrent rest pain and dynamic ST depression. Her GRACE score predicts a high 6-month mortality. She is on aspirin, clopidogrel and fondaparinux.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Coronary angiography with PCI within 72 hours
Discharge with outpatient CT coronary angiography
questions.e: High-risk UA (high GRACE) needs early coronary angiography with PCI within 24 to 72 hours.

clues: GRACE score predicts a high 6-month mortality
steps.x: **High-risk** NSTE-ACS on full medical therapy.

elim: Anatomy is not yet known; angiography comes first.
Unsafe in high-risk ACS with ongoing pain.
Contraindicated with ongoing rest pain.
Not used in NSTE-ACS.

steps.x: **A. Coronary angiography with PCI within 72 hours.** High GRACE = early angiography ± PCI within 72 hours.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with unstable angina is pain free on aspirin, ticagrelor and fondaparinux. His ECG is now normal and troponin was normal at 0 and 3 hours. His GRACE score is low. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Low-risk UA by GRACE is managed conservatively with medical therapy.

steps.x: Settled and **low risk** on GRACE.

elim: No indication in a stable low-risk patient.
Reserved for very high-risk or unstable patients.
A STEMI pathway.
Not used in NSTE-ACS.

steps.x: **A. Conservative medical management.** Low GRACE = conservative.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man is due for discharge after PCI for unstable angina. He is taking aspirin and ticagrelor. He asks how long he must take both antiplatelet drugs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Aspirin and ticagrelor for 1 month then stop both
Aspirin for 12 months and ticagrelor lifelong
Aspirin lifelong and ticagrelor for 12 months
questions.e: Secondary prevention: aspirin long-term and the second antiplatelet for 12 months, with a high-intensity statin, beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor.

steps.x: Secondary prevention after ACS.

elim: Too short; both cannot stop.
The other way round.
The second antiplatelet is usually stopped at 12 months.
Aspirin is lifelong.

steps.x: **C. Aspirin lifelong and ticagrelor for 12 months.** Aspirin lifelong, P2Y12 for 12 months.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is recovering on the ward after unstable angina. She is taking aspirin and clopidogrel. Her BP is 142/88 mmHg, pulse rate 84 bpm, LDL cholesterol 3.6 mmol/L and eGFR 80 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which combination is most appropriate to add for secondary prevention?
questions.e: After ACS: high-intensity statin, beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor alongside antiplatelets.

clues: recovering on the ward after unstable angina
steps.x: Antiplatelets in place; add the rest of **secondary prevention**.

elim: Simvastatin 10 mg is not high intensity; amlodipine is not first choice.
Not high-intensity statin; doxazosin has no prognostic role.
For heart failure or AF, not routine secondary prevention.
Warfarin has no role.

steps.x: **C. Atorvastatin 80 mg, bisoprolol and ramipril.** High-intensity statin + beta-blocker + ACEi.

questions.stem: A 58 year old lorry driver is ready for discharge after medical treatment for unstable angina. He holds a Group 2 (HGV) licence. He asks whether he can return to driving his lorry next week.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Drive cars but not lorries without telling anyone
Inform the DVLA and stop driving until assessed
No restriction if he is pain free
Return to lorry driving after 1 week
questions.e: After UA he must inform the DVLA and stop driving until assessed; Group 2 licence holders face stricter standards.

steps.x: Vocational driver after ACS.

elim: He must inform the DVLA as a Group 2 holder.
Not true; DVLA rules apply after ACS.
Group 2 standards are stricter.
Relicensing is possible after assessment.

steps.x: **B. Inform the DVLA and stop driving until assessed.** Group 2 after ACS: tell DVLA, stop until assessed.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has had chest pain at rest for 30 minutes. His ECG shows ST depression in V4 to V6 and troponin is normal at 0 and 3 hours. A medical student asks what is happening inside his coronary artery.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Plaque rupture with a partial non-occlusive thrombus
Plaque rupture with complete occlusive thrombus
Stable fixed stenosis limiting exertional flow
questions.e: Plaque rupture or erosion triggers platelet aggregation and a partial thrombus that transiently reduces flow.

steps.x: ACS with no necrosis: a **ruptured plaque** with a **partial** clot.

elim: Prinzmetal angina, not UA.
A rare cause of MI, usually in AF.
Gives STEMI with necrosis.
Stable angina.

steps.x: **C. Plaque rupture with a partial non-occlusive thrombus.** UA = plaque rupture + partial thrombus.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with unstable angina asks why her blood test for heart damage is normal when her ECG shows ST depression. Her troponin is 6 ng/L at 0 hours and 6 ng/L at 3 hours (reference <14 ng/L).
questions.q: Which best explains her normal troponin?
o: Reduced flow was too brief to cause myocyte necrosis
Troponin is released only from the right ventricle
questions.e: In UA the flow reduction is insufficient or too brief to cause necrosis, unlike NSTEMI where some necrosis occurs.

clues: 6 ng/L at 0 hours and 6 ng/L at 3 hours
steps.x: Ischaemia shown on ECG, but **no necrosis** shown on troponin.

elim: Would cause necrosis and raised troponin.
Repeated normal values are consistent.
Not a mechanism for normal troponin in ACS.
Troponin is released from any necrotic myocardium.

steps.x: **D. Reduced flow was too brief to cause myocyte necrosis.** Ischaemia without necrosis = normal troponin.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with unstable angina is given aspirin 300 mg and clopidogrel. A student asks how clopidogrel adds to the effect of aspirin.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
o: Blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor
questions.e: Clopidogrel is a P2Y12 inhibitor; with aspirin it reduces platelet aggregation at the ruptured plaque.

steps.x: Asked about the **second antiplatelet**.

elim: Dabigatran or bivalirudin.
Fondaparinux.
Warfarin.
Aspirin.

steps.x: **A. Blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor.** Clopidogrel/ticagrelor = P2Y12 blockade.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with unstable angina is on aspirin and ticagrelor. Fondaparinux is added. Her daughter asks why she needs a third blood-thinning drug.
questions.q: Which best describes how fondaparinux works?
o: Indirectly inhibits factor Xa via antithrombin
questions.e: Fondaparinux is a factor Xa inhibitor acting on the coagulation cascade, complementing antiplatelet drugs to limit thrombus propagation.

steps.x: Antiplatelets in place; fondaparinux acts on the **coagulation cascade**.

elim: Tirofiban or eptifibatide.
Ticagrelor, which she already has.
Dabigatran.
Aspirin.

steps.x: **D. Indirectly inhibits factor Xa via antithrombin.** Fondaparinux = factor Xa inhibitor (via antithrombin).

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with unstable angina asks why he must stay in hospital on several drugs when his troponin is normal and his pain has settled.
questions.q: Which best explains why unstable angina is treated as high-risk?
o: His troponin is likely to be falsely normal
Stable plaques calcify and rupture slowly
The pain is caused by pericardial inflammation
The partial thrombus can propagate to complete occlusion
Unstable angina always causes heart failure
questions.e: The unstable plaque carries a significant short-term risk of progression to full MI if the thrombus propagates.

clues: troponin is normal and his pain has settled
steps.x: No necrosis yet, but the **plaque is unstable**.

elim: Serial normal troponin is reliable.
Describes stable disease.
Pericarditis.
Heart failure is possible, not inevitable.

steps.x: **D. The partial thrombus can propagate to complete occlusion.** Unstable plaque can progress to MI.
